worlds.original_scenario: I run a small, independent charity which attempts to help people struggling with their vet costs. I have several people who pay monthly by direct debit and also receive some one off donations.
worlds.additional_information:
The treasurer is checking a £120 Faster Payment received on 16 March 2026, reference FP-0316-EL. The bank’s remitter details name Elaine Carter and her personal current account. Elaine’s email to the fundraiser says she sent the £120 from her banking app after reading about a rescued dog’s emergency treatment. The charity’s 2023 HMRC recognition letter is on file, and the treasurer’s status check confirms the charity was still recognised on 16 March 2026.

Elaine signed an electronic Gift Aid declaration on 15 March, and the e-signature service holds the signed document, timestamp and audit record. The declaration says it covers this donation, and the finance assistant matched it to FP-0316-EL through her donor record. Her tax summary for the year to 5 April 2026 shows £980 of Income Tax paid. Her signed note lists £200 of other Gift Aid donations that year; the treasurer’s sheet shows £30 recoverable on this £120 and £50 on the others, £80 in total, well below her £980.

The sales, booking and event records show nothing linked to this payment, and the only thing sent to Elaine was the standard thank-you email; she was not offered admission, advertising, a product or any other benefit. It did not go through a payroll giving scheme, and no shares, securities or other assets were delivered. An older spreadsheet groups it with two CAF card and voucher redemptions (CC-0314, VC-0317), but those were paid to the charity in a combined batch on 18 March, while FP-0316-EL came directly from Elaine’s bank on 16 March. The treasurer wants to include this receipt in the ordinary Gift Aid return if the records permit.

worlds.additional_information: Robyn Ellis paid the charity £260 on 4 February 2026. worlds.original_scenario: I run a small, independent charity which attempts to help people struggling with their vet costs. I have several people who pay monthly by direct debit and also receive some one off donations.
worlds.additional_information:
We are reviewing the £260 that reached our charity's bank account on 4 February 2026 from Robyn Ellis. The payment spreadsheet labels it 'donation', and Robyn wrote in a message that she wanted to help the animals. She has also volunteered at our adoption days. Our treasurer found two different folders under her name, so I have copied the relevant history below.

In the January events correspondence, Robyn, who runs a local grooming salon, asked whether our supporter newsletter could carry a booking link and whether the homepage could feature the salon for six weeks. The coordinator sent her a mock-up and quoted £260 for the two placements. Robyn replied that the amount worked for her. The coordinator's booking sheet shows the placements as 'awaiting settlement' until 4 February, when the £260 arrived; the same sheet then changed to 'confirmed'. The March newsletter archive and the dated website capture show the link in the agreed locations. A later volunteer note says 'we didn't raise an invoice, so I called it a donation'. A separate £20 cash gift from Robyn at the December collection event has its own receipt and was not part of the newsletter arrangement.

A draft plan to cancel the March newsletter appears in the folder, but it is marked 'not approved'; the final distribution log and archived newsletter show that the edition went out. We have the charity's HMRC recognition letter. Robyn's personal tax position and whether she completed a Gift Aid form for the £260 have not been checked. The receipt under review in this file is the February £260 entry, not her separate £20 collection gift.

worlds.original_scenario: I run a small, independent charity which attempts to help people struggling with their vet costs. I have several people who pay monthly by direct debit and also receive some one off donations.
worlds.additional_information:
Our finance volunteer is working through March receipts for our small veterinary hardship charity. The payment under review is a £95 credit dated 1 March 2026. The bank export identifies Devon Gray as the remitter from a personal account. The charity's HMRC recognition letter and a recent registration-status response confirm its recognition was still in force on 1 March 2026. Devon responded to a veterinary emergency appeal, and the booking and sales registers show no related purchase or reservation; the only thing sent to Devon was the automated thank-you email, and no discount or other benefit was offered. The remitter page identifies an ordinary bank transfer initiated from Devon's personal account, distinct from the employer deduction file, the securities transfer journal, and the charity-card and voucher processor's separately numbered settlement batch.

There is a folder labelled 'Devon tax and Gift Aid'. A P60 inside shows a substantial tax payment, but its heading says 'year ending 5 April 2024'. A separate summary from our accountant covers the charity's own 2025–26 accounts, not Devon's personal tax. We do not have a record of Devon's Income Tax or Capital Gains Tax for the year covering that payment.

The donor database contains the first page of a scanned form marked 'D. Gray' from an earlier fundraising event. The only reference visible on that page belongs to an earlier gift, and the page setting out the declaration's coverage and duration is not in the scan. The older email address on the form has not been linked to Devon's current donor record. An index suggests a longer donor declaration may once have been filed, yet the remaining pages have not been located. The team wants to include the March £95 entry in its ordinary Gift Aid reconciliation if the supporting records permit it.
